<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <!--
    The wallet's iOS code-signing entitlements. Referenced by the committed XcodeGen
    template (scripts/ios/project.yml, `entitlements > path`), so the content is
    tracked here and survives every `cargo tauri ios init` — the same treatment as
    Info.ios.plist. `just ios-template-check` guards the wiring.

    iCloud Documents (the ubiquity container) backs the user-held blob backup
    (src-tauri/src/blob_backup.rs): a content-addressed mirror of the account's
    media in the app's iCloud Drive container, user-visible in the Files app —
    the one backup layer that survives the PDS itself failing. The container id
    follows Apple's `iCloud.<bundle-id>` convention and must exist on the App ID
    (Apple Developer portal: enable the iCloud capability with this container and
    regenerate the App Store provisioning profile, or TestFlight signing fails
    with an entitlements mismatch).

    The container id is FROZEN at `iCloud.dev.malpercio.identitywallet` and must
    stay that way even after the bundle id is renamed to org.obsign.*. An iCloud
    container id cannot be renamed, and Apple permits one that does not match the
    bundle id; changing it would orphan the repo CAR snapshot and the blob mirror —
    the disaster-recovery source — silently, in an app that comes up looking like a
    clean install. See ADR-0030.
  -->
  <key>com.apple.developer.icloud-container-identifiers</key>
  <array>
    <string>iCloud.dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>
  <key>com.apple.developer.icloud-services</key>
  <array>
    <string>CloudDocuments</string>
  </array>
  <key>com.apple.developer.ubiquity-container-identifiers</key>
  <array>
    <string>iCloud.dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>

  <!--
    Keychain access groups — the decoupling that makes a bundle-id rename survivable.

    Without this key every wallet Keychain item lands in the IMPLICIT group
    `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)dev.malpercio.identitywallet`, i.e. the access group IS the
    bundle id. Renaming the bundle would make every existing item — device keys,
    Share 1, sessions, the managed-DID index — invisible, silently, with the app
    presenting as a clean install. See ADR-0030.

    ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING. iOS files a new item into the FIRST entry of this array
    when the caller does not name a group, and searches EVERY entitled group when a
    read does not name one. So:

      [0] org.obsign.shared    — the stable group. Does not track the bundle id, so a
                                 rename cannot move it. New items are written here.
                                 Also the shared group MM-419's notification keys need.
      [1] dev.malpercio.…      — the legacy group, implicit until now. Listed EXPLICITLY
                                 so it stays readable after the bundle id moves, when it
                                 would otherwise stop being implicit and vanish.

    Neither entry may be removed or reordered while any install may still hold items in
    the legacy group. `just bundle-identity-check` and keychain.rs's
    `entitlement_declares_stable_group_first` test enforce both.

    UNLIKE the iCloud container above, this needs no Apple Developer portal registration:
    `keychain-access-groups` is not an App ID capability, and a provisioning profile already
    authorizes the entire team prefix through a `<TeamID>.*` wildcard — which is why
    `org.obsign.shared` signs fine while the bundle id is still `dev.malpercio.*`. Confirm
    after any profile change with:
      security cms -D -i <profile>.mobileprovision | plutil -p - | grep -A3 keychain-access-groups
  -->
  <key>keychain-access-groups</key>
  <array>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared</string>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>
</dict>
</plist>

# reach the live delegate whose class the callbacks are installed on) and
# `UNUserNotificationCenter` (the permission prompt, whose completion handler is a `block2`
# block). Both are the same objc2 0.3 generated-bindings family already in the lockfile via the
# vendored auth-session plugin, so neither adds a major.
objc2-ui-kit = { workspace = true, features = ["UIApplication", "UIResponder", "UIApplicationDelegate"] }
objc2-user-notifications = { workspace = true, features = ["UNUserNotificationCenter", "block2"] }
# Background media-backup scheduling (bg_backup.rs): the iOS `BGProcessingTask` that keeps an
# opted-in identity's iCloud mirror topped up without opening the app. `objc2` supplies
# `Retained`/`AnyThread`; `objc2-background-tasks` the `BGTaskScheduler`/`BGProcessingTaskRequest`
# bindings; `block2` the launch + expiration handler blocks the scheduler stores. Same objc2 0.6
# family as objc2-foundation, so no duplicate major enters the lockfile. iOS-only — every other
# platform leaves the scheduling surface inert.
objc2 = { workspace = true }
objc2-background-tasks = { workspace = true, features = ["BGTaskScheduler", "BGTask", "BGTaskRequest", "block2", "dispatch2"] }
block2 = { workspace = true }
# "Wi-Fi only" background-backup check: SCNetworkReachability's IS_WWAN flag, since a
# BGProcessingTaskRequest can't require an unmetered link (bg_backup.rs).
system-configuration = { workspace = true }

[dev-dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] }
httpmock = "0.8"
tempfile = { workspace = true }
# Tests construct valid + deliberately-broken repo CARs by hand (commit + MST nodes + record
# blocks framed into CARv1) to exercise repo_backup's client-side validator. `multihash` wraps
# the SHA2-256 digest into a CIDv1 multihash on the build side; the validator itself reads CIDs
# through `cid`'s own API and never needs this crate at runtime.

I need to wire up the notification registration in the page component. When the create flow finishes, I'll call `registerForNotifications()` alongside the identity registration. But I also need to handle the import/claim flow since that also completes onboarding — both paths should trigger the notification signup.

For the re-pinning on every successful contact with Custos, I realize that needs to happen more broadly than just at completion. The pragmatic approach is to add an opportunistic sweep on app open that refreshes notification sender keys and registers for notifications across all managed identities, similar to how the backup routines run. Then also call it explicitly at create/claim/recovery completion.

Actually, registering on every app open is both correct and cheap since it's an upsert operation — and that's what triggers the AWAITING_APNS_TOKEN → REGISTERED transition once the user grants permission. Since registration itself re-pins, a single sweep handles both concerns.

So I'll create a `syncNotifications()` helper that runs through each managed DID and calls `registerForNotifications()` best-effort, which handles the re-pinning. Run it on app mount and at onboarding completion — that matches the opportunistic backup pattern and gives us the "every successful app↔Custos contact" behavior at the launch granularity without being excessive.

=== sample fragment ===
A newly created identity could finish onboarding, show "You're all set", and then not appear on the home screen. The last step of the create flow records the identity in the wallet's own list — the home screen reads from that list alone — and if that one write failed, the flow reported success anyway, nothing retried it, and the state survived force-quitting the app. The identity, its master key, and its recovery shares were never at risk, but the only way to make it visible again was to run the recovery ceremony on an identity that had not actually been lost. That step now retries, and if it still fails the app says so plainly and offers to try again instead of claiming success. Obsign also re-checks this on every launch and re-registers an identity whose create flow left it out — so an install already stuck in this state repairs itself on the next open. Identities you removed from a device on purpose are remembered as removed and are never brought back.

content.content: Custos can now send push notifications, and the first one is live: when an agent asks to act on your behalf, your phone tells you instead of the request waiting silently until you next open the app. Point your instance at a relay with `[notifications] relay` and the feature switches on; leave it unset and none of it exists — no keys are generated, no registration endpoints answer, nothing is sent. Notifications are sealed on your instance to one specific device and opened only on that device, so neither the relay nor Apple ever sees what a notification says. They also prove where they came from: your instance signs each one with a key your devices have pinned, so a relay that turned hostile could drop or repeat notifications but could never write one that looks genuine. Length is padded to fixed sizes, because how long a notification is would otherwise reveal what kind it is; anything too large to pad is dropped rather than sent in a way that leaks. Devices register over the app's normal authenticated channel and can unregister at any time, and when Apple reports a device is gone, its registration is removed at once. Deleting an account or revoking an operator device also tells the relay to forget the devices involved. Operators rotate the signing keys with `pds notification-keys` — publish a new key alongside the old, retire the old once devices have re-pinned, or revoke it outright if it is compromised.

input.content: Obsign can now receive the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. On first launch it asks permission, generates a notification key that never leaves the device, and tells each of your identities' servers where to reach it — so a notification can be sealed to your phone specifically, and opened nowhere else. Nothing about this can identify you to anyone in between: the key protects notification content only, it is never used to sign anything, and losing it costs you banners rather than an identity. Obsign also re-checks which signing keys your instance publishes every time it contacts it. That is what keeps the window short if one of those keys is ever compromised — a key your operator revokes stops being trusted by your phone the next time the two talk, without you doing anything. Registration is quiet by design: on a simulator, or for an identity hosted somewhere that runs no relay, Obsign simply carries on with notifications switched off rather than reporting an error you cannot act on. Both Obsign and Admin Companion now require iOS 17, which is where Apple's encrypted-notification support begins.

125:- `src/self_held_kit.rs` — the **escrow-less self-held Shamir kit** (5 Tauri IPC commands — "Add a recovery key" on the identity screen): the `rekey.rs` ceremony minus the escrow, for a claimed identity whose device key holds `rotationKeys[0]` but whose host is not Custos. `build_self_held_kit(did)` (generate + stage a client-side seed / 2-of-3 v2 envelope split in the per-DID `self-held-kit-staging:{did}` slot BEFORE any network call, prove eligibility, return the additive diff + the host's URL), `submit_self_held_kit(did)` (device-key-sign a PLC rotation op inserting the derived recovery key directly after the device key — the whole current tail shifts down one index, nothing is removed — POST it to plc.directory, write Share 1 to the per-DID iCloud-synchronizable slot with read-back verify, refresh the cached log + doc, record the `{did}:self-held-kit` marker; biometric-gated in the frontend), `confirm_self_held_kit(did)` (teardown gate mirroring `confirm_rekey`: Share 1 must be verifiably durable before the staging slot — the last local home of Shares 2 and 3 — is destroyed), `self_held_kit_in_progress_cmd(did)`, and `self_held_kit_escrow_offer_cmd(did)` (the upsell **seam**: true only when the marker is present AND the identity's *current* host advertises `escrow`, so it is never true right after a kit completes). **Share 1 → Keychain; Shares 2 AND 3 → the user** — with no escrow there is no third party, and the sovereign recovery path already reconstructs from any two. **plc.directory is the only peer for anything touching the identity** (audit-log read, op submit, cache refresh); the sole request reaching the hosting PDS is the public, unauthenticated `describeServer` capability probe that proves the host offers no escrow — often served from the `pds_capabilities` cache, carrying no share material and no credential. No session, no `/v1/*` call, hence no `SESSION_LOCKED` and no `ESCROW_FAILED` in the error surface; user-facing copy must say "no share is sent to your server", never "your server is never contacted". `guard_self_held_kit_op` is the SEVENTH strict wallet allowlist and deliberately drops `guard_rekey_op`'s "current rotationKeys must be exactly 2" rule (which encodes the pre-inversion Custos `[device, PDS]` layout and would reject every claimed identity): device key pinned at `[0]`, the fresh recovery key inserted at `[1]`, the tail preserved verbatim, verificationMethods / services / alsoKnownAs byte-identical. `SelfHeldKitError` (NOT_DID_PLC, WALLET_NOT_AUTHORIZED, HOST_OFFERS_ESCROW, RATE_LIMITED, GUARD_REJECTED, INVALID_AUDIT_LOG, SHARE_GENERATION_FAILED, SIGNING_FAILED, PLC_SUBMISSION_FAILED, PLC_DIRECTORY_ERROR, SHARE_STORAGE_FAILED, SHARE_NOT_STORED, NETWORK_ERROR, IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND) serialized as `{ code: "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE" }` with camelCase fields

input.new_string:
- The four **notification** Keychain accounts are app-global, not per-DID (`notifications::NOTIFICATION_ACCOUNTS` is the inventory, and `keychain.rs`'s `notification_material_never_syncs` reads that constant rather than a copy of it): `notification-device-uuid` (the stable identifier the server keys registrations on — it must outlive every identity that uses it, which is why it is not the transient `devices.id`), `notification-key-priv` (the raw P-256 scalar), `notification-sender-keys` (the versioned per-host pin document), and `notification-apns-token` (lowercase hex). The private key and the pin document are written under **`kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`** via `keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock`; the other two use ordinary `store_item`. **None of them ever syncs** — the private key most pointedly, since it is readable on a locked screen and syncing it would place a passcode-free key in the Apple account for no recovery benefit (a replacement device mints its own on first registration). The pin document is read **fail-open** (corrupt ⇒ empty), the deliberate inverse of `ceremony-staging`: it holds public keys the server re-serves on the next contact, so refusing to read it would forfeit the very re-pin that repairs it
- `keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock` is **not a third store**. It writes into the same device-local store as `store_item` and is read by the same `get_item`/`delete_item`; only the item's protection class differs, and one account written through both accessors is one record whose class is the last write's. The write is delete-then-add rather than the crate's add-or-update, because `SecItemUpdate` cannot change an existing item's protection class — an update would silently keep whatever class the first write set, which is the one thing this accessor exists to control. `keychain::Accessibility` + `accessibility_of` are test-only, since iOS never reports a class back and the in-memory double is the only place the locked-screen readability is assertable
- `NotificationsError` variant names serialize as SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE with camelCase fields to the frontend -- the TypeScript `NotificationsError` union in `$lib/ipc` must match exactly (SESSION_LOCKED, RATE_LIMITED, IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND, KEY_GENERATION_FAILED, KEYCHAIN_ERROR, SERVER_ERROR, NETWORK_ERROR); `SESSION_LOCKED` carries `reason: UnlockReason`, the cue to run `unlockIdentity(did)` and retry. `RegistrationStatus` is a bare SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE union (`REGISTERED` / `AWAITING_APNS_TOKEN` / `UNSUPPORTED`) and the notification IPC types (`RegistrationOutcome`, `SenderKeyPinning`, `SenderKey`, `NotificationDiagnostics`) serialize with `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`; their `$lib/ipc` counterparts must match exactly. Neither notification command is biometric-gated — nothing is signed and no identity material is exposed, and a prompt on the onboarding-completion path would be a demand the user cannot connect to anything they did

## Key decisions

- **Toolchain scripts are SHARED, design is forked.** The iOS toolchain scripts
  (`scripts/ios-env.sh`, `ios-postinit.sh`, `ios-check.sh`) are thin wrappers over the
  single shared implementation in the repo-root `scripts/ios/` (each wrapper pins this
  app's dir and the `admin` recipe prefix), and the Xcode-project workarounds come from
  the SHARED XcodeGen template `scripts/ios/project.yml` (rendered on every
  `cargo tauri ios init` via `bundle > iOS > template`), so neither the script logic nor
  the project workarounds can diverge between the two app lanes. This app's framework
  list lives in its `tauri.conf.json` `bundle > iOS > frameworks` — just
  `SystemConfiguration`; no AuthenticationServices, this app has no in-app OAuth
  plugin. The
  OKLCH token *architecture* is forked from identity-wallet — but the token *values*,
  components, and product/design briefs are this app's own terminal-native register.
  See the root `apps/identity-wallet/AGENTS.md` for the full explanation of every iOS
  patch and the toolchain seam; it is the single source of truth for those gotchas
  (this app reuses the same swift-rs `[patch.crates-io]`).
- **Excluded from the Linux CI gate** (`just ci-pds`) like identity-wallet: it needs the
  Apple `security-framework` toolchain. Built/checked on macOS via `just admin-*`.
- **Grotesk UI font is provisional** (system SF Pro via `--font-sans`) until the
  `/impeccable` font pass; JetBrains Mono (the signature voice) is bundled in `static/fonts/`.
- **App icon: `app-icon.svg` is the source of truth** (brand rationale in DESIGN.md §6);
  `app-icon.png` is its 1024×1024 render and the input `cargo tauri icon` consumes.

1	// pattern: Mixed (Functional Core pin-store arithmetic; Imperative Shell commands + Keychain)
2	//
3	// The device half of the end-to-end-encrypted notification relay: the keys a Custos instance
4	// seals push payloads to, the registration that tells it where to send them, and the pinned
5	// sender-key set the Notification Service Extension verifies against.
6	//
7	//   register_for_notifications(did)         — POST /v1/notifications/register
8	//   refresh_notification_sender_keys(did)   — GET  /v1/notifications/sender-keys (the re-pin)
9	//   get_notification_diagnostics()          — what this device holds, for Settings
10	//
11	// Nothing here decrypts anything. The extension that does is a separate target (a later phase);
12	// this module's whole job is to leave the right material in the right Keychain slots under the
13	// right protection class, and to keep the pinned set fresh.
14	//
15	// # Why the material is device-global rather than per-DID
16	//
17	// A push arrives at the extension as `{v, kid, enc, ct}` and nothing else — no DID, no handle,
18	// no account hint, because naming one would hand the relay and Apple the metadata the whole
19	// design exists to withhold. So the recipient key cannot be per-identity: the extension would
20	// have no way to choose among several. One device, one notification keypair, one `device_uuid`;
21	// every identity on the device registers the same public key with its own host.
22	//
23	// # Why the pinned set is per-host anyway
24	//
25	// `kid` is an autoincrement column on *one* Custos instance. Two instances will both publish a
26	// `kid` of 1 for entirely unrelated keys, and this wallet routinely holds identities on more
27	// than one. So the pin store is a map from hosting server to that server's published set, and
28	// the extension tries every candidate key registered under the incoming `kid`. That costs
29	// nothing and cannot go wrong: HPKE Auth mode either authenticates against a given sender key
30	// or it does not, so a wrong candidate fails closed and the next is tried. A single flat set
31	// keyed by `kid` alone would instead have two instances silently overwriting each other.
32	//
33	// # Re-pinning is wholesale replacement
34	//
35	// A successful fetch replaces that host's entry entirely rather than merging into it. That one
36	// choice is what implements all three rotation semantics from the design: a new key appears, a
37	// retired key stays as long as the server keeps publishing it, and a *revoked* key vanishes from
38	// this device the first time it contacts its Custos. Merging would keep a compromised key
39	// pinned forever, which is precisely the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close.
40	//
41	// A failed fetch changes nothing. An instance that answers 501 has not revoked anything — it has
42	// switched the feature off, or was never configured — and a 503 means it could not read its own
43	// keys. Treating either as "revoke everything" would let one bad deploy strip the pins off every
44	// device that happened to check in during it.

The functions `record_apns_token` and `hex_encode_apns_token` are only used in iOS-specific code and tests, so they're being marked as dead code in the library build. There's also a complexity warning about a type definition, and a suggestion to use `std::slice::from_ref` instead of cloning in one of the test cases. Let me pull up the exact Clippy output to see the full details and address each issue properly.

 ('store_pins_for_host("https://a.example.com", &[a.clone()])','store_pins_for_host("https://a.example.com", std::slice::from_ref(&a))'),
 ('store_pins_for_host("https://b.example.com", &[b.clone()])','store_pins_for_host("https://b.example.com", std::slice::from_ref(&b))'),
 ('store_pins_for_host("https://pds.example.com", &[fresh.clone()])','store_pins_for_host("https://pds.example.com", std::slice::from_ref(&fresh))'),
 ('store_pins_for_host(&host_key(&server.base_url()), &[stale.clone()])','store_pins_for_host(&host_key(&server.base_url()), std::slice::from_ref(&stale))'),
 ('store_pins_for_host(&host_key(&server.base_url()), &[pinned.clone()])','store_pins_for_host(&host_key(&server.base_url()), std::slice::from_ref(&pinned))'),
]
for old,new in subs:
    n=s.count(old)
    assert n>=1,(old,n)
    s=s.replace(old,new)

# hex/record are only reached from the iOS bridge (and the tests) — mirror bg_backup's gating.
s=s.replace(
"""/// Record the APNs device token iOS handed us, reporting whether it actually changed.""",
"""/// Record the APNs device token iOS handed us, reporting whether it actually changed.

s=s.replace("pub(crate) fn record_apns_token(", "#[cfg(any(target_os = \"ios\", test))]\npub(crate) fn record_apns_token(",1)
s=s.replace("pub(crate) fn hex_encode_apns_token(", "#[cfg(any(target_os = \"ios\", test))]\npub(crate) fn hex_encode_apns_token(",1)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
print("ok")
PY

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && git add -A && git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Wallet: notification keys, registration and sender-key re-pinning (MM-419)

The device half of the encrypted notification relay MM-418 landed the server
side of. Obsign generates a per-device P-256 notification key, registers it with
each identity's Custos, and re-pins the sender keys that instance publishes.

Three things are worth reviewing carefully.

**The keychain surface is an accessibility class, not a new store.** The shared
access group already exists — `org.obsign.shared` is first in the entitlement
array, so every item already lands somewhere a Notification Service Extension
can reach. What the extension additionally needs is
`kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, because a push arrives on a locked screen.
`store_item_after_first_unlock` writes into the *same* device-local store as
`store_item` and is read by the same `get_item`; the write is delete-then-add
because `SecItemUpdate` cannot change an existing item's protection class, and
the class is the whole contract. The class is confined to notification material:
it opens content, signs nothing, and is on the never-sync deny list.

**The pinned sender-key set is keyed by hosting server.** `kid` is an
autoincrement column on one instance, and two instances will both publish a
`kid` of 1 for unrelated keys — which this wallet, holding identities on
several hosts, would silently collapse into one entry. The extension will try
every candidate under an incoming `kid`; HPKE Auth mode fails closed on a wrong
sender key, so trying costs nothing.

**A successful fetch replaces a host's set wholesale.** That single choice is
what implements the design's rotation semantics: a key the operator revokes
disappears from the device at its next contact. Merging would keep a compromised
key pinned forever, which is the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close.
A 501 or 503 changes nothing — neither is a revocation, and clearing on one
would strip every device that checked in during a bad deploy.

The APNs bridge is iOS-only and adds the two device-token delegate methods to
Tauri's delegate class rather than swizzling: `class_addMethod` fails if the
selector already exists, and declining is the outcome we want if Tauri ever
implements them itself. Everything with logic worth testing lives in
`notifications.rs` instead, since the bridge is only ever compiled by the
cross-compile lane and only ever exercised on a device.

Both apps move to iOS 17, where CryptoKit's HPKE API begins.

Registration reports "no APNs token yet" and "this host runs no relay" as
outcomes rather than errors, so the onboarding-completion call has nothing to
catch on a simulator or for an identity hosted on a standard PDS.

Not verified without a device: the delegate installation, the permission prompt,
and that a real token round-trips. The iOS cross-compile is the only automated
check those paths get.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

Phase 5 of [MM-311](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311)'s notification relay — the device half of what [#467 (MM-418)](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/467) landed on the server. Obsign generates a per-device P-256 notification key, registers it with each identity's Custos over the normal authenticated channel, and re-pins the sender keys that instance publishes.

Linear: [MM-419](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-419/notify-59-wallet-notification-keys-registration-sender-key-re-pinning)

## Three decisions worth reviewing

**The keychain surface is an accessibility class, not a new store.** The shared access group already exists — `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` is first in the entitlement array, so every item already lands somewhere a Notification Service Extension will be able to reach. What the extension additionally needs is `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, because a push arrives on a locked screen and the extension has no way to present a biometric prompt. So `keychain::store_item_after_first_unlock` writes into the **same** device-local store as `store_item`, is read by the same `get_item`/`delete_item`, and differs only in the item's protection class — the module docs say this explicitly, because the existing two-store split trains the eye to read "another accessor family" as "another store".

The write is delete-then-add rather than the crate's add-or-update: `SecItemUpdate` cannot change an existing item's protection class, so an update would silently keep whatever class the first write set — and the class is this accessor's entire contract. The relaxation is confined to notification material, which opens content and signs nothing; all four slots are on the never-sync deny list, the private key most pointedly (it is readable without the passcode, so syncing it would put a passcode-free key in the Apple account for no recovery benefit).

**The pinned sender-key set is keyed by hosting server.** `kid` is an `AUTOINCREMENT` column on *one* instance, and two instances will both publish a `kid` of 1 for entirely unrelated keys — which this wallet, routinely holding identities on more than one host, would silently collapse into a single entry. The design doc's flat set glosses over this. The extension will try every candidate registered under an incoming `kid`; HPKE Auth mode either authenticates against a given sender key or does not, so a wrong candidate fails closed and trying costs nothing.

**A successful fetch replaces a host's set wholesale.** That one choice is what implements all three rotation semantics: a new key appears, a retired key stays while the server still publishes it, and a *revoked* key vanishes from the device the first time it contacts its Custos. Merging would keep a compromised key pinned forever, which is precisely the window re-pin-on-every-contact exists to close. A 501 (host runs no relay) or 503 (instance cannot read its own keys) changes nothing — neither is a revocation, and clearing on one would strip the pins off every device that happened to check in during a bad deploy.

## The rest

- **APNs bridge (`apns.rs`, iOS-only).** iOS delivers the token to two `UIApplicationDelegate` methods and exposes it nowhere else, so the bridge installs those methods on Tauri's live delegate class. **Add, never swizzle**: `class_addMethod` fails if the selector already exists, and that failure is the one we want — Tauri does not implement either today, and silently displacing its implementation if it ever did would be much worse than declining and logging. On a *changed* token it re-registers every managed identity; an unchanged one (iOS re-delivers every launch) does nothing.
- **Ordinary "no" answers are outcomes, not errors.** `AWAITING_APNS_TOKEN` (simulator, denied prompt, or a token that has not arrived yet) and `UNSUPPORTED` (a 501) come back as statuses, so the onboarding-completion call has nothing to catch on a simulator or for an identity on a standard PDS.
- **Cadence.** `registerForNotifications(did)` fires at each onboarding flow's completion (create / claim / recovery) and once per app open per identity, fire-and-forget alongside the existing opportunistic backup passes. Registration re-pins on the same contact, so one call does both.
- **iOS 17 for both apps** (`bundle > iOS > minimumSystemVersion`), where CryptoKit's HPKE API begins. Previously both rode tauri-cli's 13.0 default. Neither app has an installed base below 17.
- **`aps-environment` entitlement** added to the wallet. Unlike `keychain-access-groups`, this one **does** need Apple Developer portal work: enable Push Notifications on the App ID and regenerate the provisioning profile, or TestFlight signing fails with an entitlements mismatch.

## Dependencies

`objc2-ui-kit` and `objc2-user-notifications` (both 0.3, the same generated-bindings family as `objc2-foundation`) become direct iOS-only deps. Both were already in the lockfile transitively via the vendored auth-session plugin, so no new major enters the tree; `cargo deny` is green.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p identity-wallet` | 718 passed (34 new across `notifications`/`keychain`) |
| `cargo clippy -p identity-wallet --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo build --lib --target aarch64-apple-ios` (both apps) | clean |
| `pnpm check` / `pnpm test` (wallet) | 0 errors · 236 passed (7 new harness tests) |
| `pnpm check` (admin-companion) | 0 errors |
| ticket-ref · docs · changelog · bundle-identity · ios-template · capability · bruno · font · deny · lock | all pass |

The harness half of the acceptance criterion is covered by `src/lib/harness/notifications.test.ts`, which drives the three states a browser can genuinely be in (no token, no relay, working Custos) plus the wholesale-replacement property. The keychain specifics — including the protection class each slot lands under — are asserted in Rust against the in-memory double, since a browser has neither a Keychain nor APNs.

**Not verified without a device:** the delegate-method installation, the permission prompt, and that a real APNs token round-trips into a registration. The iOS cross-compile is the only automated check those paths get, and MM-420's on-device demo is where they first run for real.

content.text:
MM-419 is done — [PR #472](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/472) is open and Linear is in **In Review** with the PR attached.

## What shipped

**[notifications.rs](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/notifications.rs)** — the device half: stable `device_uuid`, per-device P-256 notification keypair, per-host pinned sender-key set, registration against `POST /v1/notifications/register`, and the re-pin against `GET /v1/notifications/sender-keys`.

**[apns.rs](apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/apns.rs)** — iOS-only device-token bridge (permission prompt, delegate callbacks, re-register on token change).

Plus the keychain accessor, IPC wrappers, harness fakes, flow wiring at all three onboarding completions + app open, iOS 17 for both apps, `aps-environment`, docs, and a changelog fragment.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Two places where the issue's framing and the codebase disagreed, and the code won:
- The issue calls the keychain work a "shared access group (net-new surface)". It isn't — ADR-0030 already made `org.obsign.shared` the write target for *every* item. The net-new thing is the **protection class**, and the subtle trap there is that `SecItemUpdate` can't change one, so add-or-update would silently keep whatever class the first write set. Delete-then-add isn't a style choice; it's the only way the accessor's contract holds across the re-pin that rewrites the set on every contact.
- The design doc describes one flat pinned set. That breaks on a multi-identity wallet, because `kid` is an `AUTOINCREMENT` column *per instance* — two Custos hosts both hand out `kid: 1`. Keying by host is safe precisely because HPKE Auth mode fails closed, so the extension can try candidates without a disambiguator.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Verification

718 Rust tests (34 new), clippy clean, iOS cross-compile clean for both apps, `pnpm check` 0 errors, 236 frontend tests (7 new harness tests), and all ten script gates pass.

Two things I want to flag rather than bury:

1. **Not verified without a device.** The delegate installation, the permission prompt, and a real APNs token round-tripping have no automated check beyond the cross-compile. That's inherent to the surface, but it means the feature is compile-proven, not behaviour-proven, until MM-420's on-device demo.
2. **Apple Developer portal work is required before this can build signed.** The `aps-environment` entitlement needs Push Notifications enabled on the App ID and the provisioning profile regenerated — otherwise TestFlight signing fails with an entitlements mismatch. Unlike `keychain-access-groups`, the team-prefix wildcard doesn't cover it.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

I'm checking each of the nine cases against the actual code to build a disposition table. The first one involves `mint_device_uuid` in notifications.rs where the read-back is skipped—if the store operation returns success but doesn't actually persist, the next launch would mint a fresh UUID, creating orphaned server rows. I need to trace through whether `store_item` properly maps OS errors or if there's a gap in the error handling.

Actually, looking closer: the key writer already does a read-back for exactly this reason, and it's cheap. If the read-back fails, we error out entirely, which blocks registration—arguably worse than proceeding with a UUID that might not stick. But the module's own documentation is explicit about avoiding dead rows, and erroring is the honest approach: we couldn't establish a stable identifier. The subtlety is that `device_uuid()` handles corrupt or empty reads by minting a replacement, so a failed read-back is fail-closed and consistent with the key writer's pattern. I'll accept this one.

Now moving to the second case: `PRRT_...MgD2` about a 32-byte-but-invalid scalar wedging permanently. I need to verify that `stored_notification_scalar` returns Some only for exactly 32-byte values and trace what happens when that gets passed to the keypair derivation.

For the third case around concurrent re-pin lost updates: the sync `store_pins_for_host` function can't yield mid-execution, but on Tauri's multi-threaded tokio runtime, two concurrent tasks on different threads can execute it simultaneously, creating a genuine data race on the keychain document. The critical detail is that test-mode uses a thread-local keychain store.

In production, the real Keychain is shared across threads, so the race is genuine. The suggested mutex approach using `std::sync::Mutex` works since `Mutex::new` is const in Rust 1.63+. And since `+page.svelte` calls `syncNotifications` in a loop without awaiting, this is definitely reachable. Accept the mutex.

For the fourth case around clock failure causing NETWORK_ERROR: that's valid and aligns with my own stated invariant.

The remaining issues are straightforward: explaining the identity graft in the test is a cheap fix, and the sixth case about inferring relay support from `sovereignSessions` is a legitimate catch—the real 501 comes from the relay config being unset, which is independent of sovereign sessions, so using it as a proxy couples the logic unnecessarily and prevents modeling scenarios like Custos with sovereign sessions but no relay.

For the seventh issue about the diagnostics tying key ID to APNs token, the Rust code derives the notification key ID independently of the token, so the harness diverges there—I should add a `notificationKeyMinted` flag to the harness state to model this correctly.

The eighth issue is about re-registration after a migration: when an identity moves to a new Custos instance, that instance has no registration yet and its sender keys aren't pinned, so re-registration is genuinely needed. This fits the design's key lifecycle—migrations count as a completion event that should trigger re-enrollment. I need to find the right DID variable to use.

For the ninth issue about the changelog's privacy claim, I'm re-reading my statement that "nothing about this can identify you to anyone in between" and realizing that's overclaiming—I need to be more precise about what the notification key actually protects. ify the assumptions in issue #6 about what the server can actually do, then trace through the +page.svelte branches to see how the DID variable flows through the migration.

input.content: Obsign can now receive the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. On first launch it asks permission, generates a notification key that never leaves the device, and tells each of your identities' servers where to reach it — so a notification can be sealed to your phone specifically, and read nowhere else. What that protects is the notification's *content*: neither the relay in the middle nor Apple can see what one says. It does not hide that a notification happened — your own server is told which device to reach, and Apple necessarily handles delivery — so what is kept from everyone in between is the message, not the fact of it. The key is used for nothing else: it never signs anything, and losing it costs you banners rather than an identity. Obsign also re-checks which signing keys your instance publishes every time it contacts it. That is what keeps the window short if one of those keys is ever compromised — a key your operator revokes stops being trusted by your phone the next time the two talk, without you doing anything. Registration is quiet by design: on a simulator, or for an identity hosted somewhere that runs no relay, Obsign simply carries on with notifications switched off rather than reporting an error you cannot act on. Both Obsign and Admin Companion now require iOS 17, which is where Apple's encrypted-notification support begins.

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && git add -A && git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Address CodeRabbit review on MM-419

Nine threads, all verified against the code before acting on. Six were real
defects, two were harness fakes that diverged from the backend they stand in
for, and one was copy that overclaimed.

**Two ways the notification key could get stuck.** A stored scalar of the right
*length* but the wrong *value* (zero, or past the curve order) returned
`KeyGenerationFailed` on every call forever, since nothing else overwrites that
slot — while a wrong-*length* one three lines away self-healed. Both are equally
unreconstructable, so both now mint a replacement. Separately, `mint_device_uuid`
skipped the read-back its sibling key writer performs: a write that reports
success without persisting mints a fresh uuid next launch, accumulating exactly
the dead server row and live relay handle per app start the doc says this must
prevent.

**A concurrent re-pin could restore a revoked key.** Every host's pinned set
lives in one keychain document and `store_pins_for_host` did an unsynchronized
load-modify-store. `+page.svelte` fires a registration per identity without
awaiting, and Tauri's runtime is multi-threaded, so two of those overlap for
real. Losing the later write is not just a stale entry: if the discarded pass
was the one that dropped a revoked sender key, that host goes back to trusting
it. A `std::sync::Mutex` around the read-modify-write closes it, taken and
released inside the synchronous function so it never crosses an `.await`.

**A migration left the destination silent.** Moving an identity to a new Custos
gives it a server that has never seen this device — no registration, no pinned
keys — until some future relaunch happened to run the app-open sweep. Both
migration branches now re-register.

An unavailable clock was reported as `NETWORK_ERROR`, against the rule stated at
the top of the same file; it is a `ServerError { status: None }` now.

**Harness fidelity.** Two fakes inferred state instead of tracking it. Relay
support was read off the `sovereignSessions` capability, which made "a Custos
with sovereign sessions but no relay" unreachable and misdescribed the wire —
the server's 501 comes from `[notifications] relay` being unset, and Custos
advertises no notifications capability at all, so this is now its own state
flag rather than an invented capability string. And diagnostics reported the
key id only while an APNs token was present, where the real command reads the
Keychain scalar and never consults the token; a device that registered and later
lost its token shows a key on device and null in the harness, which is what a
Settings surface would have been written against.

The changelog claimed "nothing about this can identify you to anyone in
between". Encryption protects the notification's content; it does not hide that
one was delivered, and the server is told which device to reach. Reworded to
claim only what is true.

Declined: the MD041 "no top-level heading" lint on the changelog fragment —
every fragment in changelog.d/ is a bare paragraph by convention.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push 2>&1 | tail -3
